```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)

# Screenshots live in vignettes/images (excluded from the package build to keep
# it small) and are read from GitHub when the images are not available locally
screenshot <- function(file) {
  path <- file.path("images", file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    path <- paste0(
      "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DillonHammill/DataEditR/master/",
      "vignettes/images/", file
    )
  }
  knitr::include_graphics(path)
}
```

**DataEditR** is an R package that makes it easy to interactively view, enter, filter and edit data. The data editor is a shiny application built on the MIT-licensed [Tabulator](https://tabulator.info) JavaScript library, so it stays fast with large datasets, and it can edit tables stored in a database as well as data in your R session. In this vignette we will explore the key features that are available through the `data_edit()` function.

## Preparation

In order to get started with **DataEditR**, we will need to install the package from CRAN and load it into our current R session:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("DataEditR")
library(DataEditR)
```

If you would like to use the development version of **DataEditR** it can be installed directly from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github("DillonHammill/DataEditR")
```

## 1. Data Visualisation

Simply supply your data in the form of a matrix, data.frame, tibble or data.table to `data_edit()` to view it in an interactive table. For example, if we wanted to take a look at the `mtcars` dataset:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("editor.png")
```

The data editor has four parts:

* the **header** with the *Cancel* button, the name and size of the data, and the *Done* button;
* the **toolbar** to open other data, undo and redo changes, show or hide columns, see active filters, find values, review changes, see the code that reproduces your edits, export the data and see the keyboard shortcuts;
* the **grid**, which shows the row indices on the left, a type badge (`abc` for text, `123` for numbers, `date`, `T/F` for logicals) next to each column name, and a filter box under each column name;
* the **status bar** showing how many rows and columns are on screen, a summary of the selected cells and a summary of your changes.

The data editor will open in an RStudio `"dialog"` box by default, but can be optionally displayed in the RStudio viewer pane or a web browser by setting `viewer` to `"pane"` or `"browser"` respectively. The size of the dialog box is controlled by `viewer_width` and `viewer_height`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          viewer = "browser")
```

Row names (such as the car names in `mtcars`) are moved inside the table to a frozen `row names` column so that they can be edited, and the row indices are always displayed on the left-hand side to aid navigation. Only the visible rows are drawn in the browser, so scrolling through 100,000 rows is as smooth as scrolling through 10.

Once you are finished, close the data editor by hitting the `Done` button in the top right corner and the edited data will be returned. If you wish to discard all changes made to the data, select the `Cancel` button in the top left corner and the unedited data will be returned instead (or the value supplied to the `cancel` argument).

## 2. Data Import

`data_edit()` can read in any form of tabular data from file for viewing and editing. By default `data_edit()` will use `read.csv` from the `utils` package to read in files, but this can be changed to any reading function by supplying the name of the function to the `read_fun` argument. If you need to pass any additional arguments to your reading function, these can be supplied as a named list to the `read_args` argument.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mtcars <- data_edit("mtcars.csv",
                    read_fun = "read.csv",
                    read_args = list(header = TRUE,
                                     row.names = 1))
head(mtcars)
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
head(mtcars)
```

The name of an object in your R session can also be supplied as a character string, e.g. `data_edit("mtcars")`.

### 2.1 Open other data without leaving the editor

The `Open` menu in the toolbar switches to other data without having to close the data editor. You can load any data frame, matrix or `dbplyr` table from your R session by name, upload a file (read with `read_fun` and `read_args`) or create a new empty table with a chosen number of rows and columns.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("open-menu.png")
```

## 3. Data Manipulation

`data_edit()` provides a variety of spreadsheet-style tools to edit your data. We will explore the use of each of these tools below. Many of them can be reached through the keyboard; press `?` inside the data editor or click the `?` button in the toolbar to see the full list of shortcuts.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("editing.gif")
```

### 3.1 Edit cells

Double-click a cell to edit it, then press `Enter` to save the new value or `Esc` to cancel. Values are checked against the type of the column: numbers are stored as numbers, dates as dates and `TRUE`/`FALSE` as logicals. Typing `NA` or clearing a cell stores a missing value.

If you type something that does not fit a number or date column, `data_edit()` asks what you would like to do instead of silently converting the whole column to text. You can store a missing value, convert the column to text or cancel the edit.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("type-guard.png")
```

### 3.2 Select, copy, paste, clear and fill

Click and drag (or `Shift` + click) to select a range of cells. The status bar shows the sum, mean and count of the selected numbers, just like a spreadsheet. Selected cells can be copied (`Ctrl+C`) and pasted (`Ctrl+V`) within the data editor or to and from other software such as Excel, cleared with `Delete`, or filled down with the value in the first row of the selection (`Ctrl+D`). A paste, fill or clear is a single step that can be undone. Click a column header to select the whole column.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("range.png")
```

### 3.3 Undo and redo

Every change can be undone with `Ctrl+Z` (or the undo button in the toolbar) and redone with `Ctrl+Y`. This includes edits, pasted ranges, added or removed rows and columns, renamed columns and changes reverted from the review panel.

### 3.4 Addition or removal of rows or columns

Rows or columns can be added to the data from within the data editor by right clicking on a cell or a column header. This will display a context menu with the options to insert rows above or below, delete the selected rows, fill down, or rename, insert, hide or delete columns.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("row-menu.png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("column-menu.png")
```

New rows can also be added to the end of the data with the `+ Add row` button under the grid, and new columns with the `+` button after the last column header. New columns start empty and their type is worked out from the values you enter when the data is returned.

To prevent users from adding or removing rows or columns, set `row_edit = FALSE` or `col_edit = FALSE` respectively.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          row_edit = FALSE,
          col_edit = FALSE)
```

### 3.5 Rename rows or columns

`data_edit()` has full support for editing row and column names. Double-click a column header (or choose `Rename column` from its menu) to rename it; the new name must be unique and cannot be empty. Row names are edited like any other cell in the `row names` column. The row indices cannot be edited.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("rename.png")
```

To prevent users from editing column names, set `col_names = FALSE` or supply the names of the columns that cannot be renamed. For example, if we only wanted to prevent users from renaming the `mpg` column:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_names = "mpg")
```

### 3.6 Resize columns

To resize columns, go to the right-hand border of the header of that column and drag the cursor to the desired width.

### 3.7 Find values

Press `Ctrl+F` or click `Find in data` to search the rows and columns on screen. The first matching cell is selected and the number of matches is shown (e.g. `1 of 7`); press `Enter` to jump to the next match, `Shift+Enter` to go back and `Esc` to clear the search.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("find.png")
```

### 3.8 Append columns or rows

`data_edit()` can perform `rbind` and `cbind` operations internally to append new rows or columns to the data prior to editing. The new rows or columns can be supplied as a matrix or data.frame, a named list or, for empty rows or columns, a vector of names to the `row_bind` or `col_bind` arguments. If binding both rows and columns, it is important to note that rows are bound before columns.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# New column to add
new_col <- matrix(rep(NA, nrow(mtcars)),
                  ncol = 1,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, "test"))

# Edit data with new column added
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_bind = new_col)

# Add two empty rows and an empty column called "notes"
data_edit(mtcars,
          row_bind = c("New car 1", "New car 2"),
          col_bind = "notes")
```

### 3.9 Read-only and hidden columns

If you would like to prevent values from being edited in certain columns, you can supply the names of the columns that cannot be edited to the `col_readonly` argument. Read-only columns show a lock next to their name, and their values and names cannot be changed. For example, if we wanted to prevent the `mpg` column from being edited:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_readonly = "mpg")
```

Columns that users should not see at all can be supplied to `col_hide`. Hidden columns cannot be viewed or edited, but they are kept in place in the returned data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_hide = c("vs", "am"))
```

### 3.10 Factor columns

`data_edit()` fully supports data frames with factor columns. Factor columns are converted to character for editing so that you can freely enter new values without encountering errors. When the editor is closed, character columns are converted to factors if `col_factor = TRUE` is set.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Create data with factor column
df <- data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"),
  group = factor(c("A", "B", "A"))
)

# Edit - factor columns are handled automatically
df_edited <- data_edit(df, col_factor = TRUE)
```

## 4. Data Creation

You can also use `data_edit()` to interactively create data.frames from scratch without any coding.

### 4.1 Start with empty template

If no data is supplied to `data_edit()` an empty data.frame will be constructed with 10 rows and columns. You can then build your data.frame from scratch by adding new rows and columns and annotating the cells.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit()
```

The dimensions of the template can be controlled by supplying a vector of the form `c(nrow, ncol)` to indicate the number of rows and columns to use.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c(20, 15))
```

### 4.2 Start with a labelled template

Alternatively, you can pass a vector of column names to create a data.frame template with pre-defined column names. Use `+ Add row` to add as many rows as you need.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("Date", "Country", "Temperature", "Rainfall", "Visibility", "Humidity"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("template.png")
```

The columns of a template are typed automatically when the data is returned, so a column in which you only entered numbers is returned as a numeric column.

## 5. Data Filtering

`data_edit()` makes it easy to view and edit a subset of your data: filter rows by typing under the column headers and show or hide columns from the `Columns` menu. Edits made to a subset are applied directly to the complete dataset.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("filtering.gif")
```

### 5.1 Row filtering

Every column has a filter box under its name and the box depends on the type of the column:

* **numbers** have `min` and `max` boxes to keep values within a range;
* **columns with a few distinct values** (e.g. `cyl` or `gear`) have a list to pick one or more values (`Any` means no filter);
* **text** columns keep values that contain what you type.

Rows must match every filter to be shown. Active filters are listed as chips in the toolbar; click the `x` on a chip to remove that filter or `Clear filters` to remove them all. The status bar shows how many of the rows are on screen.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("filters.png")
```

### 5.2 Column selection

Click `Columns` in the toolbar to show or hide columns, or choose `Hide column` from the menu of a column header. `Show all` and `Hide all` change every column at once, and the button shows how many columns are visible.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("columns-menu.png")
```

### 5.3 Edits apply to the complete dataset

Filtered rows and hidden columns are only *views* onto your data, so any change you make while a filter is active is made directly to the complete dataset, without requiring any additional action. Rows added while a filter is active stay visible until the filters change.

### 5.4 Return or export data subsets

`data_edit()` will return the complete dataset as an R object for downstream use by default. If you would like to return just the rows and columns that are on screen, open the menu next to the `Done` button and choose `Only what's on screen` before pressing `Done`. The menu shows the size of the data that each option returns.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("done-menu.png")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mtcars_subset <- data_edit(mtcars)
str(mtcars_subset)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
mtcars_subset <- mtcars[mtcars$cyl %in% c(4, 6) & mtcars$mpg >= 20,
                        c("mpg", "cyl", "disp", "hp", "wt", "gear", "carb")]
str(mtcars_subset)
```

## 6. Data Saving

`data_edit()` will automatically return the edited data with appropriate column classes as an R object for use within R. Matrices, tibbles and data.tables are returned with their original class, and the type of each column is kept: numbers stay numbers, dates stay dates and text that looks like a number (e.g. `"001"`) stays text. Character columns are not converted to factors by default, but this can be changed by setting `col_factor = TRUE`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Add character column
mtcars_new <- cbind(rownames(mtcars), mtcars)
colnames(mtcars_new)[1] <- "car"

# Convert characters to factors
mtcars_new <- data_edit(mtcars_new,
                        col_factor = TRUE)
str(mtcars_new)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
mtcars_new <- cbind(rownames(mtcars), mtcars)
colnames(mtcars_new)[1] <- "car"
mtcars_new$car <- factor(mtcars_new$car)
str(mtcars_new)
```

The edited data can also be written to a file of any format by specifying the name of the file to the `save_as` argument and specifying the name of the writing function to use through `write_fun`. The default is to use `write.csv` from the `utils` package. You can also pass any additional arguments to your write function in a named list to `write_args`. The data will be written to file when the `Done` button is selected; untick `Also save to` in the `Done` menu to close the editor without saving.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mtcars_new <- data_edit(mtcars,
                        save_as = "mtcars.csv",
                        write_fun = "write.table",
                        write_args = list(sep = ",",
                                          row.names = TRUE))
```

Alternatively, data can be downloaded to file at any time from the `Export` menu in the toolbar, either all data or only what is on screen. Files are named after `save_as` (with `-subset` added for subsets), or after today's date if `save_as` is not supplied, and are written with `write_fun` and `write_args`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("export-menu.png")
```

## 7. Complex user inputs

`data_edit()` can also be used to accept complex inputs from users and these inputs can be restricted by adding columns with checkboxes, dropdown menus, date pickers or password fields. To use this feature, the options for the columns must be supplied in a named list through the `col_options` argument. Columns with options can still be renamed, and users can still add or remove other columns.

### 7.1 Checkboxes

Checkboxes can be used to obtain `TRUE` or `FALSE` value inputs from users. Double-click a checkbox cell to change its value; ticked cells are returned as `TRUE`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_bind = "fast",
          col_options = list(fast = c(TRUE, FALSE)))
```

### 7.2 Dropdown menus

Dropdown menus can be used to help prevent typing errors when a set number of options are available for a column. For example, if we have a factor with levels `Treatment-A`, `Treatment-B` or `Treatment-C` it would be easier to select these options from a dropdown menu instead of having to manually type them. Dropdown menus can be added in the same way as checkboxes.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Add column for car colour
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_bind = "colour",
          col_options = list(colour = c("red",
                                        "blue",
                                        "orange",
                                        "green",
                                        "black")))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-options.png")
```

### 7.3 Dates

Dates can be entered interactively by selecting the relevant day from a calendar. To convert a column to accept interactive date inputs, supply a list with the name of the column and `"date"` as the option to `col_options`. The column is returned as a `Date` column.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("date", "time", "region", "temperature"),
          col_options = list(date = "date"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-options-date.png")
```

### 7.4 Passwords

If you would like to keep your data entries a secret, you can convert relevant columns to accept passwords as inputs. The data is entered as per usual, but the values are displayed as dots to conceal the entered data. To convert a column to accept password inputs, supply a list with the name of the column and `"password"` as the option to `col_options`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("date", "time", "user", "password"),
          col_options = list(password = "password"))
```

## 8. Customisation

`data_edit()` has been designed to be simple, but does come with some customisation options including column stretching, addition of logos and/or titles, custom themes and the option to hide the menus.

### 8.1 Stretch columns to fill page

If you would like to make full use of the space available to you, you can set `col_stretch = TRUE` to stretch the columns to fill the full width of the display.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(iris,
          col_stretch = TRUE)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("stretch.png")
```

### 8.2 Logo and title

`data_edit()` does also have support for adding a logo and/or title to the data editor. For example, if you wanted to use `data_edit()` within your own package you can customise it with your package `logo` (the path or URL of an image) and instructions to the user through `title`. Use `logo_size` to set the width of the logo in pixels and `logo_side` to place it on the `"left"` or `"right"` of the title.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
logo <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DillonHammill/DataEditR/master/man/figures/logo.png"
data_edit(mtcars,
          logo = logo,
          logo_size = 26,
          title = "Car data")
```

### 8.3 Custom themes

`data_edit()` uses Bootstrap 5 through the `bslib` package. You can explore the different themes by supplying the name of a [Bootswatch](https://bootswatch.com/) theme to the `theme` argument. Alternatively, you can create your own custom `bs_theme` and supply that object to `theme` instead.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Preset theme
data_edit(
  mtcars,
  theme = "flatly"
)

# Custom theme
library(bslib)
custom_theme <- bs_theme(
  version = 5,
  primary = "#7C3AED",
  base_font = font_google("Lato")
)
data_edit(
  mtcars,
  theme = custom_theme
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("custom.png")
```

### 8.4 Simplified editor

Set `hide = TRUE` to hide the `Open` and `Export` menus and the options of the `Done` button, for example when `data_edit()` is used to collect data from users. When `save_as` is supplied the data is still written to file when `Done` is pressed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("Name", "Email", "Attending"),
          col_options = list(Attending = c(TRUE, FALSE)),
          save_as = "rsvp.csv",
          hide = TRUE)
```

## 9. Reviewing and tracking changes

`data_edit()` keeps track of every change you make, so you can see what has changed before you hit `Done` and revert any change on its own.

### 9.1 Review changes

The status bar summarises your changes (e.g. `2 cells edited · 1 row added`) and the `Review changes` button shows how many changes there are. Click it to open the review panel, which lists every edited, added, removed or renamed cell, row and column with its old and new value. Click the name of a row to jump to it in the grid, `Revert` (or `Remove` / `Restore`) to undo that one change, or `Revert all` to go back to the original data. Reverts can be undone with `Ctrl+Z` like any other change.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("reviewing.gif")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("review.png")
```

### 9.2 Highlight changed cells

Set `track = TRUE` to highlight cells that have been edited or added compared to the original data with a blue tint. Any cell whose value differs from the original, as well as all cells in newly added rows or columns, will be highlighted. Highlights follow undo, redo and reverts, and inserting rows or columns does not cause other cells to appear changed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          track = TRUE)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("track.png")
```

You can pass any valid CSS color to `track` to customise the highlight colour. For example, to use red:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          track = "red")
```

## 10. Keyboard shortcuts

| Action                  | Shortcut                      |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Edit cell               | Double-click                  |
| Save / cancel edit      | `Enter` / `Esc`               |
| Undo / redo             | `Ctrl+Z` / `Ctrl+Y`           |
| Select a range          | Click and drag, `Shift`+click |
| Copy / paste range      | `Ctrl+C` / `Ctrl+V`           |
| Clear selected cells    | `Delete`                      |
| Fill down               | `Ctrl+D`                      |
| Find in data            | `Ctrl+F`, then `Enter` / `Shift+Enter` |
| Rename column           | Double-click header           |
| Row and column menus    | Right-click                   |
| Show the shortcuts      | `?`                           |

Use `Cmd` instead of `Ctrl` on a Mac.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("shortcuts.png")
```

## 11. RStudio Add-in

`DataEditR` also ships with an RStudio add-in should you prefer to interact with your data in this way. Simply highlight the name of a dataset in an active script or the console and select `Interactive Data Editor` from the list of `Addins` in your RStudio session. If nothing is highlighted, an empty table is opened instead. The add-in can be bound to a keyboard shortcut through `Tools > Modify Keyboard Shortcuts...`.

## 12. Databases

`data_edit()` can also edit tables stored in a database. Connect with `DBI`, pass a `dbplyr` lazy table (optionally filtered) to `data_edit()` and the rows are loaded into the editor. Changes are staged while you edit and written to the database in a single transaction when you press `Done` and confirm the summary of changes.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "cars.sqlite")

data_edit(tbl(con, "cars") %>% filter(cyl == 6))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("db-commit.png")
```

See `vignette("databases", package = "DataEditR")` for how to connect to different databases, how rows are matched to the database and what happens when someone else changes the data while you are editing it.

## 13. Interactively Edit Googlesheets

`DataEditR` can also be used to interactively edit googlesheets using `googlesheets4`. Simply authorise `googlesheets4`, create a new sheet, edit the data using `data_edit()` and write the edited data to the created sheet.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(googlesheets4)

# Authorise
gs4_auth(
  email = "username@gmail.com"
)

# Create a sheet
ss <- gs4_create(
  "mtcars"
)

# Edit data
mtcars_new <- data_edit(
  mtcars,
  save_as = ss,
  write_fun = "write_sheet",
  write_args = list(sheet = "mtcars")
)
```

## 14. Exporting Code

For reproducibility, it is possible to export the code required to generate the final edited version of your data. The generated code uses tidyverse-style `dplyr` verbs to transform the original data into the edited version.

### 14.1 See the code as you edit

Click `Code` in the toolbar to see the code that reproduces your edits so far. The code updates as you edit and can be copied with the `Copy` button.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("code.png")
```

### 14.2 Print code to console

Set `code = TRUE` within `data_edit()` to print the generated code to the console when you press `Done`. The code uses `dplyr` verbs such as `rename()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `slice()`, and `tibble::add_row()` to replicate your edits. Copying and pasting this code into the console will recreate the edited version of your data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          code = TRUE)
```

For example, renaming a column, modifying a cell value, removing a row and adding a new row might produce code like:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(dplyr)

mtcars <- mtcars %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = ".rownames") %>%
  rename(horsepower = hp) %>%
  slice(-5) %>%
  mutate(
    mpg = replace(mpg, 1, 21.5),
    horsepower = replace(horsepower, 3, 95)
  ) %>%
  tibble::add_row(.rownames = "My car", mpg = 26, cyl = NA, disp = NA,
                  horsepower = NA, drat = NA, wt = NA, qsec = NA, vs = NA,
                  am = NA, gear = NA, carb = NA) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames(var = ".rownames")
```

For database tables the code uses `rows_update()`, `rows_append()` and `rows_delete()` to make the same changes to the database.

### 14.3 Save code to file

Alternatively, users can get `DataEditR` to automatically create a new R script to store this code by providing a name for the R script to `code`. For example, the below code creates a new R script called `mtcars_edit.R` and inserts the code required to programmatically generate the final edited version of your data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          code = "mtcars_edit.R")
```

### 14.4 Using `data_code()` directly

The `data_code()` function can also be used outside of `data_edit()` to generate code from any pair of original and edited data frames:

```{r}
library(DataEditR)

# Original data
x <- data.frame(
  A = c(1, 2, 3),
  B = c("x", "y", "z"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Edited data (changed a value and renamed a column)
x_edit <- data.frame(
  A = c(1, 5, 3),
  Beta = c("x", "y", "z"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Generate code
cat(data_code(x, x_edit, name = "x"))
```

## 15. Shiny modules

The data editor is also available as a shiny module, so you can add an editable table to your own shiny applications with `dataEditUI()` and `dataEditServer()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(DataEditR)

ui <- fluidPage(
  dataEditUI("edit")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  edited <- dataEditServer("edit", data = reactive(mtcars))
  observe(print(head(edited())))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

See `vignette("shiny-modules", package = "DataEditR")` for the options of the module and how it works with the other modules in **DataEditR**.

## Summary

**DataEditR** is a powerful and interactive tool to make your data viewing, entry, filtering and editing as seamless as possible. If you need any help or encounter any issues with **DataEditR** please let me know by posting an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/DillonHammill/DataEditR/issues).
